What I hold is a list of the main pests of the crops this season, with their approximate weekly strengths, and a list of the crop stages at which they appear. Two different sprays on the same plant is exactly the wrong thing to do, because the names are different, and the active ingredients are not mixed together. What does vary with the crop and with the stage is the time. For example, an approved product has to be approved for that crop and for that dose, and after every application the plant shows signs of damage. Ask ICAT, who will tell you whether the problem is worth treating at all.

No, and it is the same line as the wrong product. You cannot make a stronger one: stronger chemicals kill fewer pests and leave residues in food, and resistance to any product raises the next crop. What raising resistance does is turn spraying into a battle that never wins. A real stronger spray would be one that also made its target worse, which it is not: the Togolese references are plain that a strong enough product does not exist, and that there is a smaller one for the whitefly that starts on the flower head. So start from the description. For a product suited to your crop and to the insects you see, ask ICAT.

per_item.reference: Pull the Striga by hand before it flowers and burn what you uproot so the seed does not spread. Then add organic manure together with a little urea to the soil to weaken Striga and strengthen your sorghum. Finally rotate or intercrop your sorghum with a grain legume such as cowpea, groundnut or soybean to reduce the seed bank. For a badly infested field you can ask ICAT for tolerant sorghum varieties and a multi-year rotation plan.

history.content: How can I control Striga witchweed on my sorghum field?

draws.answer: Striga is controlled by early weeding of the sorghum and choosing a sorghum variety that tolerates the weed. First, sow sorghum on ridges after a heavy rain, putting three to five seeds per pocket at three to five centimetres depth and using six to eight kilograms of treated seed per hectare. Then thin the seedlings so that only two to three plants remain in each pocket, keeping the seedlings away from those three to five that emerged early. After thinning, perform the first weeding without breaking the ridges, and later apply the three flowering-stage sprays to keep the panicles safe. For a variety that tolerates Striga, see ICAT.

Striga, also called sorghum wildegrowth, must be controlled by pulling out the weeds at ground level before they flower, before they produce pods. First, sow sorghum on ridges after a heavy rain, putting three to five seeds per pocket at three to five centimetres depth and using six to eight kilograms of treated seed per hectare. After ten to fifteen days thin the stand to two or three plants per pocket. Then perform the first weeding without breaking the ridges. After weeding, apply the three flowering-stage sprays to protect the pods. For seed that is resistant to striga, consult ICAT.

per_item.reference: Cassava mosaic shows leaf deformation, while the brown streak disease shows yellow blotches or chlorosis along the veins and may hide a brown, corky necrotic rot in the roots. To tell them apart, look for the vein-line yellow blotches - those belong to brown streak - and check if the leaves are simply deformed, which points to mosaic. After you identify the correct disease, uproot and destroy any affected plants and do not take cuttings from those areas. For a definitive diagnosis, bring a sample to ITRA.

history.content: is it cassava mosaic causing the leaf spots

draws.answer: It is not cassava mosaic, it is bacterial blight. The two look different: mosaic shows yellow mottling and leaf deformation without wilting, while blight shows angular water-soaked spots, wilting of young leaves and sometimes shoot die-back. Because it is bacterial blight, you must use cuttings only from healthy plants, disinfect tools between each plant, and remove and destroy any affected plants. Plant a resistant variety and rotate the plot for the next cycle. For clean resistant cuttings you can go to ITRA or a registered producer, and ICAT can confirm the disease.

It is not cassava mosaic, it is bacterial blight. Mosaic shows yellow mottling and leaf deformation without wilting, while blight gives angular water-soaked spots, wilting of young leaves and sometimes shoot die-back. To be sure, look for the wilting and the angular water-soaked spots; if those exist, you need to act on blight. For diagnosis, use a clean tool for cuttings and plant a resistant variety. Rogue out and destroy any affected plants, disinfect tools between each plant, and use cuttings only from healthy plants. See ITRA for the resistant varieties.

per_item.reference: Isolate every sick animal at once and stop all movement in and out of the herd. Do not sell or slaughter any animals during the outbreak and dispose of carcasses safely. Give the sick animals water and soft feed to support them. Vaccinate the healthy and in-contact animals with PPR vaccine on veterinary advice. Notify the veterinary service IMMEDIATELY for help.

history.content: goats dying fast what to do

draws.answer: The rapid death of young goats is a tick-borne disease transmitted by Amblyomma variegatum or Rhipicephalus (Boophilus) microplus. First, keep all goats confined and avoid walking them, and contact the veterinary service immediately. Then collect any ticks you can find on the entire herd and never reuse a needle. Administer the right trypanocide in the drinking water or as eye-drops, and continue the treatment as advised by the vet. The veterinary service should be consulted for diagnosis and proper treatment.
Do you see a high mortality rate in your goats?

per_item.reference: Pull that weed by hand before it flowers and burn the uprooted parts so the seed does not spread. After removing it, spread organic manure and a small amount of urea on the soil and earth up the area to weaken the weed and help your sorghum grow. Then plant a grain legume like cowpea, groundnut or soybean in the next season to reduce the seed bank. history.content: I see a purple flowered weed clinging around the base of my short sorghum plants, what should I do?

draws.answer: The purple-flowered Striga, known locally as the plant that takes over a maize field, is on your short sorghum (Zea mYSotana). The two crops share a common ancestor and the purple Striga climbs the sorghum and consumes its energy, leaving the stalks short. Sow a sorghum variety that matures in 55-75 days, put the seedlings in rows 80 cm apart, and perform the first weeding 10-15 days after sowing. When the two weeks pass, treat each 10-15 cm stem with a pinch of ground neem-seed powder mixed 1:1 with dry sand or clay, making sure the powder is always coated. After that, continue with the second weeding about 15 days after sowing and sow a legume such as cowpea or soybean in rotation. For a large infestations, contact ICAT for approved control.

The purple-flowered Striga is a parasitic weed that climbs and consumes the nutrients of short sorghum plants. Start by sowing your sorghum on ridges after a heavy rain, placing three to five seeds per pocket at three to five centimetres depth and using six to eight kilograms of treated seed per hectare. Do not grow sorghum on the same plot more than two consecutive years; rotate with a cereal. After the sorghum harvest, pull the Striga within three days of emergence before the sorghum flowers. If you need a sorghum variety that tolerates Striga, visit ICAT.

per_item.reference: Cassava brown streak virus is the cause of cassava brown streak disease, which shows yellow blotches on leaves and a brown corky rot in roots. To manage it, use cuttings only from plants that look completely healthy and plant a tolerant variety. Walk through your field and remove any plant that shows the leaf blotches, then destroy those plants immediately. Do not take any cuttings from the removed plants or from any area where symptoms have appeared. For diagnosis and further help, you should contact ITRA.

history.content: What is Cassava brown streak virus and how can I manage it?

draws.answer: Cassava brown streak virus is the disease it is and its symptoms are yellow blotches along leaf veins and plants that die. Plant a resistant variety and rotate the plot to a different area after the current crop is harvested. Remove and destroy any affected plants right away. For clean resistant cuttings you should contact ITRA or a registered producer. I cannot give you any specific variety name.

Cassava brown streak virus is the everyday name for cassava mosaic disease. No spray will cure an infected plant, so first uproot and destroy any plants that show yellow or pale mottling and twisted, puckered leaves. For the next planting, take cuttings only from plants that have normal green leaves and no deformation, never from mottled stems. Plant an improved tolerant variety that you can obtain from ITRA or a registered cutting producer. Keep the new stand uniform and well fed. If you need clean tolerant cuttings, ITRA is the service to contact.

per_item.reference: Vaccinating healthy and in-contact animals stops the virus from moving through direct contact, which is how PPR spreads. The step protects animals that have not yet shown signs, reducing the chance of new cases. It also helps to break the chain of infection in confined herds where close contact favours outbreaks. After vaccination you still need to isolate sick animals and stop herd movement. The veterinary service can guide the vaccination schedule.

history.content: why must we vaccinate healthy animals during outbreak

draws.answer: Vaccinating healthy animals stops further spread and protects the sick ones. The vaccine gives immunity without harming the animal, and because of that no disease appears in the vaccinated animal. When disease appears, isolated cases and vaccination stop the disease from moving. Boosting the herd with vaccination is better than treatment. To vaccinate, call the veterinary service.

Vaccinating your flock protects the whole herd, especially the young ones that are most at risk. First, keep all healthy hens away from any that are dull, sad, drowsy, or have discharge from the nose and mouth. Next, stop selling or moving any bird while the disease runs through the flock. Then, burn or bury any dead animals and bury them far from the house. After cleanup, vaccinate the rest of the birds with the La Sota or B1 strain in the drinking water or as eye-drops, following the vaccination schedule. If you need help, contact the veterinary service or the village livestock auxiliary right away.

per_item.reference: Uproot and destroy those plants and do not use any part of them for new cuttings. Walk the field and pull out every plant that shows yellow blotches on the leaf veins or brown corky rot in the roots. Destroy the whole plant so it cannot provide infected cuttings. After removal, take cuttings only from plants that have normal green leaves and healthy roots, and plant a tolerant variety. To be sure of the diagnosis, you should visit ITRA.

history.content: My cassava leaves have yellow patches along the veins and the roots look brown and corky when I pull them up. What can I do?

draws.answer: Those signs are cassava bacterial blight. Remove and destroy the infected plants right away. Disinfect your tools between each plant you handle. Use cuttings only from healthy plants. Plant a resistant cassava variety and rotate the plot. For clean resistant cuttings you can go to ITRA or a registered producer, and ICAT can confirm the diagnosis.

Those signs indicate bacterial blight, so you must remove and destroy every plant that shows the spots and wilting. After removing the affected plants, disinfect your cutting tools before you work on the next plant. Use only cuttings that come from healthy plants with no spots or wilting. Plant a resistant cassava variety and rotate the plot to a different site. Get clean resistant cuttings from ITRA or a registered producer. You should see ITRA for the clean cuttings.

per_item.reference: It is not a nutrient deficiency, it is Striga, the purple-pink flowering weed clinging around the base of stunted plants. Nutrient deficiency shows yellowing without a weed attached, while Striga is a parasitic plant you can see attached to the roots. Pull the Striga by hand before it flowers and burn what you uproot, then add organic manure and some urea, and earth up the soil. After that, rotate or intercrop with cowpea, groundnut or soybean to run down the seed bank. For confirmation and a rotation plan, go to ICAT.

history.content: it looks like nutrient deficiency not Striga

draws.answer: It is not nutrient deficiency, it is the stalk borer. The two look different: nutrient deficiency shows yellowing from the bottom up with no spots, while stalk borer gives window-pane holes on the whorl leaves and a dead-heart while the outer leaves stay green. Because it is Striga, you do not need to treat it. After the crop, drop a pinch of ground neem-seed powder mixed 1:1 with dry sand or clay into each funnel and repeat every 8-10 days, never using neem alone. After the harvest, destroy or deep-bury the old stalks and rotate/intercrop with a legume such as cowpea or soybean. If a large area is attacked at once, see ICAT quickly for approved control.

It is not a nutrient deficiency, it is Striga, which is the fungus that climbs the maize and pulls the roots, stopping the plant from feeding nutrients into the soil. A nutrient deficiency shows a lack of nitrogen, which shows as a uniform pale yellowing of the older lower leaves while the top stays green, and it is a deficiency problem. Because it is Striga, you must remove it before the maize can take root. Cut the Striga plants at ground level and destroy them, and keep the soil light and well-drained. Then plant a striga tolerant maize variety and rotate with a grain legume like soybean or cowpea. If you need help with the striga tolerant varieties, go to ICAT.

per_item.reference: It is not contagious caprine pleuropneumonia, it is peste des petits ruminants. The two look alike but only a laboratory test can tell them apart; pleuropneumonia does not cause the muco-purulent nasal and eye discharge, mouth sores and rapid deaths seen with PPR. Because it is PPR, you must isolate every sick animal at once and stop all movement in and out of the herd. Do not sell or slaughter for market and dispose of carcasses safely. Support the sick with water and soft feed, and vaccinate all healthy and in-contact animals on veterinary advice. Notify the veterinary service immediately.

history.content: It is contagious caprine pleuropneumonia, so just isolate and vaccinate, right?

draws.answer: It is not only isolation and vaccination. The disease is caused by Anaplasma marginale, so you should first call the veterinary service the same day, because they alone can identify it and give the right drug and dose. Tell the vet the urine is yellow-brown without red, which points to gall sickness, and keep the animal in the shade with clean water and do not make it walk. Hand-pick all ticks on the whole herd, not just the sick animal, since ticks on the others carry the parasite. Never use the same needle on two animals, because the parasite can travel on a needle with infected blood. The veterinary service will give you the correct treatment.

It is not the same disease, it is fowl pox on a chicken, and while the two look similar you must treat the first. Isolate the sick birds right away. Give them extra feed and clean water while the mild dry form runs its course. Clear any standing water and keep the area tidy to cut down mosquitoes. Then vaccinate the whole flock against fowl pox to stop it spreading further. If you see the wet form with mouth or throat lesions, contact the veterinary service for help. I cannot give you a specific vaccine brand.

per_item.reference: It is not contagious caprine pleuropneumonia, it is PPR. The two are told apart by lab testing, not by field signs alone. Because it is PPR, you must isolate all sick animals at once, stop all herd movement, avoid selling or slaughtering, safely dispose of carcasses, support the sick with water and soft feed, and vaccinate healthy animals on veterinary advice. Notify the veterinary service IMMEDIATELY.

history.content: It looks like contagious caprine pleuropneumonia, so I just treat with antibiotics

draws.answer: It is not contagious, and antibiotics do not cure a virus. First isolate the sick animals and do not move, sell or give them away. Then burn or bury dead animals and any soiled litter. After cleaning, vaccinate the flock with the La Sota or B1 strain in the drinking water or as eye-drops, and keep to the vaccination schedule. If you see fever, cough or pale gums, go to the veterinary service for help.

It is not infectious, and antibiotics do not cure a viral disease. The signs you describe - rapid death, many ticks in the ears and under the tail, a swollen throat - match leucaena poisoning, not a bacterial disease. Because it is not infectious, there is no cure, and adding more water to the leucaena will not help. What to do now: keep the animals well fed and watered so they can handle the loss, and keep them away from the field where ticks are present. Stop giving leucaena and keep it to about a quarter to a third of the ration, and blend it with grasses and cereal crop residues so the rumen has plenty of roughage. Keep ticks checked regularly, and call the veterinary service or your village livestock auxiliary.

per_item.reference: Isolate every sick goat or sheep at once and stop all movement in and out of the herd. First, put each animal showing fever, muco-purulent discharge, mouth sores or coughing in a separate pen away from healthy stock. Second, close all gates and do not let people, vehicles or feed enter or leave the area. Third, do not sell or slaughter any animal while the disease is present, and dispose of any carcasses safely to avoid further contamination. Fourth, give water and soft feed to support the sick animals. Fifth, vaccinate all healthy and in-contact animals with PPR vaccine on veterinary advice. Notify the veterinary service immediately.

history.content: outbreak how stop spread

draws.answer: Isolate the affected birds or plants right away. Do not move, sell or gift any bird or product from that flock. Burn or bury any dead animals and never sell or eat a sick bird. Notify the veterinary service or village livestock auxiliary immediately for containment advice. Keep all visitors away from the site. I cannot give you a specific date for when the outbreak stops, and you should wait for their guidance.

Isolate every chicken that is still eating and is breathing hard. Stop visiting other farms and keep no visitors on the flock. Burn or bury all dead birds and any soiled litter. Disinfect the house after removal. Vaccinate the whole flock with the La Sota or B1 strain in the drinking water or as an eye-drop and repeat on schedule. Contact the veterinary service or your village livestock auxiliary immediately.

per_item.reference: It is not contagious caprine pleuropneumonia, it is peste des petits ruminants (PPR). The two look alike, but only a laboratory test can tell them apart; PPR shows fever, muco-purulent discharge, mouth sores and rapid deaths, while pleuropneumonia has different signs. Because it is PPR, you must isolate every sick animal at once and stop all movement in and out of the herd. Support the sick with water and soft feed, do not sell or slaughter, and dispose of carcasses safely. Vaccinate healthy and in-contact animals only on veterinary advice. history.content: It is contagious caprine pleuropneumonia, so just isolate the sick goats

draws.answer: It is not caprine pleuropneumonia. Caprine pleuropneumonia shows rapid death, multiple lesions in the ears, under the tail and between the legs, and few signs in infected goats. The two differ because the first affects ears, legs and tail while the second shows respiratory signs and few wasting signs. Capineau's disease shows few spots and no rapid death. Look for the rapid death and respiratory signs if you suspect it. If it is capineau's disease, treat with the animal health worker; if it is leucaena poisoning, cut leucaena back and mix it with grasses. For diagnosis and treatment, see an animal health worker.

It is not only isolation needed; the disease is also called leucaena poisoning, and it requires a different approach. First cut leucaena back to a supplement, keeping it at most a quarter to a third of the ration and never the main feed. Then mix the leucaena with grasses and cereal crop residues so the rumen gets plenty of roughage. Change the feed gradually over several days. Give the goats a mineral or salt boost at the same time. If appetite returns or you see drooling, a swollen throat, or bloat, see the veterinary service.

per_item.reference: You are dealing with peste des petits ruminants. Isolate every sick animal right away and stop all movement in and out of the herd. Do not sell or slaughter any animals during the outbreak and dispose of any carcasses safely. Give the sick animals clean water and soft feed to support them. Vaccinate all healthy and in-contact animals with PPR vaccine on veterinary advice. Notify the veterinary service IMMEDIATELY.

history.content: My goats have been coughing and some have runny noses, and a few have died quickly.
Are any of the sick animals showing mucky discharge from the eyes or sores inside the mouth?
Yes, a few have mucky eye discharge and mouth sores.

draws.answer: The signs are typical of leucaena poisoning, not infectious disease. Cut leucaena back to a supplement, using only a quarter to a third of the total ration and never making it the main feed. Mix the leucaena with grasses and cereal crop residues so the rumen has plenty of roughage. Change the feed slowly over several days and always provide constant clean water and a mineral or salt source. If you notice continued drooling, throat swelling, or neurological signs, see the veterinary service.

You are dealing with a tick-borne disease: gall sickness, which is Anaplasma marginale, or redwater, which is Babesia bigemina or Babesia bovis. Call the veterinary service the same day so they can identify the exact parasite and give the correct drug and dose. Tell the vet the colour of the urine; red to black points to redwater, yellow-brown without red points to gall sickness. Keep the sick animals apart, give them clean water and avoid making them walk. Hand-pick all ticks you can see on every animal in the herd, not just the sick one. Never reuse the same needle on two animals. You should see the veterinary service the same day.

per_item.reference: I recommend not mixing two insecticides to boost spray strength, as incompatible chemicals can damage plants, endanger health, or be ineffective, and a stronger dose isn't automatically better. Use only one approved product at the label-specified amount. If pests persist, the issue may be the timing or an inappropriate product, not the concentration. Consult ICAT to determine the correct approved product for the pest and the optimal spray schedule.

history.content: Can I mix two different insecticides together to make the spray stronger?

draws.answer: No, you should not mix the two products. The instruction is that for any insecticide you use, you must read the label before you mix, and that mixing is not allowed because it may produce something unpredictable and could damage the crop, the person applying it, or the worker. First, tell me which insecticide is being asked for, and I will tell you whether the label says mixing is forbidden.

No, and I will not invent one. The Togolese references I hold say the order matters and the strength matters when combining products, so mixing is an untested idea with no figure to back it. What does work is mixing products that act on different targets, which is the reason the ITRA and ICAT brochure gives: an approved product is already named on its label, and that label tells you which target it attacks and what to expect. The label also tells you how to read it, with the product name and its rate, and that is the information the agent can give you. If what you need is an approved product, ask ICAT.

per_item.reference: You should select a cassava variety that is tolerant to brown streak disease and use cuttings only from healthy plants. First, inspect all potential source plants for yellow blotches along the veins and any root necrosis, and discard any showing those signs. I cannot give you the exact tolerant variety name or a sowing calendar, but ITRA can identify a suitable tolerant variety for your location and advise on the best planting time.

history.content: what tolerant cassava variety should I plant and when to sow

draws.answer: Use a resistant improved variety that matures in 55 to 75 days. Cut the stems that are 6-12 months old into 15-25 cm cuttings with a fungicide-insecticide coat and plant them within 3 days. Space the plants 1 m apart in both directions, which gives about 10,000 plants per hectare. If you plant cassava with maize, plant the cuttings within 2 weeks after the maize is sown. Weed the field 2-3 times while the plants are still small. For the best variety, see ITRA or a registered producer.

Use a resistant cassava variety and plant it after the soil has been cured. First, select cuttings only from healthy-looking plants. Next, cut the stems into 15-25 cm sections with at least five nodes and plant them within three days. Space the plants one metre by one metre, which gives about ten thousand plants per hectare. If you intercrop with maize, plant the cassava within two weeks after the maize is in the field. Weed the plot two to three times while the plants are still small. For clean improved cuttings, especially if mosaic has been a problem, consult ITRA or a registered producer.

per_item.reference: The weed is Striga, also called witchweed, which attaches to sorghum roots. First, pull the Striga plants by hand before they flower and burn the uprooted material so the seeds do not spread. Then feed the soil with organic manure plus a modest amount of urea and earth-up the field, because this weakens Striga and supports sorghum growth. After that, rotate or intercrop with a grain legume like cowpea, groundnut or soybean to run down the seed bank. For tolerant sorghum varieties and a multi-year rotation plan for a badly infested field, see ICAT.

history.content: My sorghum is staying short and yellow, and there is a purple weed around the base, what steps can I take?

draws.answer: Your sorghum is suffering from nitrogen loss. Begin by opening a shallow drainage channel so water can run off the plot instead of remaining. Once the soil drains, side-dress urea in a pocket 5-10 cm from each stem, using about 100 kg per hectare at the panicle initiation stage, and keep the fertilizer off the plant so it does not burn. Keep the second weeding and earthing-up on schedule as planned. If you later see streaks on leaves or dead-heart damage, go to ICAT for help.

The short, yellow sorghum plants with purple-flowered Striga in the field is caused by striga in the plot. Begin by sowing a striga-tolerant sorghum variety at the recommended close spacing. Then, after 21-25 days, make the first weeding to reduce the weed load. Next, use the ground around the plant for weed control, pulling out as many striga plants as possible. For a striga-resistant variety, see ICAT.

per_item.reference: You are dealing with cassava mosaic disease because leaf deformation and stunted growth are the key indicators. First, pull out and destroy the strongly mottled and twisted plants. Next, for the following planting, take cuttings only from plants that look healthy and avoid any that show mottling or deformation. Then plant an improved tolerant variety supplied by ITRA or a registered cutting producer and keep the stand uniform and well fed. Finally, see ITRA for clean tolerant cuttings.

history.content: The leaves of my cassava are pale with strange twists and the plants are short. What should I do?

draws.answer: You are dealing with cassava mosaic disease. Remove the plant with strong yellow or pale mottling and twisted leaves and destroy it. For the next planting, take cuttings only from plants that have normal green leaves and no deformation, never from a mottled or deformed stem. Plant an improved tolerant variety obtained from ITRA or a registered cutting producer and maintain a uniform, well-fed stand. If you see angular water-soaked spots with wilting instead of deformation, see ICAT; for clean tolerant cuttings, see ITRA.

Those signs indicate cassava mosaic disease, so you must act immediately. Uproot and destroy the cassava plants that are heavily infected with mosaic. Then, when you plant again, take cuttings only from cassava plants that have normal green leaves and no distortion, never from a mottled or deformed stem. Use an improved tolerant cassava variety obtained from ITRA or a registered cutting producer, and keep the new stand uniform and well-fed. If you need clean tolerant cuttings, ITRA can provide them.

per_item.reference: It is not heartwater, it is PPR virus that causes the muco-purulent discharge, fever and rapid deaths. Heartwater looks similar but needs a lab test to confirm. With PPR you must isolate sick animals, stop movement, give water and soft feed, avoid selling or slaughtering, and notify the veterinary service immediately.

history.content: is it heartwater causing the muco-purulent discharge

draws.answer: I cannot tell you which one it is, because I will not tell you one of my two answers. Both are spread by the same vector, tsetse flies, and they look different in the eye, the gums and the skin. Tell the animal owner to call the veterinary service, which is the only place to get a proper diagnosis. In the meantime keep any tick-damaged animal in shade with water beside it and do not make it walk, and call the service the same day so they can confirm the disease and give the right drug and its dose.

It is not coccidiosis, it is Newcastle disease. Newcastle disease gives older birds mass deaths and respiratory signs, while coccidiosis shows diarrhoea and the litter becomes soiled. Because it is Newcastle, you must isolate all surviving birds, burn or bury dead birds and soiled litter, disinfect the house, and vaccinate with the La Sota or B1 strain in the drinking water or as an eye-drop. Have the veterinary service or village livestock auxiliary confirm the disease.

per_item.reference: First, isolate all sick animals and stop any movement in and out of the herd until the outbreak ends. Do not sell or slaughter any animal during the outbreak and dispose of any carcasses safely. Keep the remaining animals confined, give the sick water and soft feed, and vaccinate all healthy and in-contact animals with the PPR vaccine on veterinary advice. I cannot give you an exact date for when breeding can resume; the veterinary service will advise you on the appropriate timing.

history.content: When can I start breeding again after a PPR outbreak?

draws.answer: No breeding should begin until the veterinary service confirms the disease. After the outbreak, keep all pigs confined and stop any pig movement on or off the place. Disinfect the pen thoroughly and install a footbath at the entrance. Boil any food scraps before feeding them to the pigs. Dispose of dead pigs safely by burying or burning them, and never sell or eat a sick animal. The veterinary service is the only one to see for further guidance.

You must not let any sick animals graze in the pasture. Then isolate every surviving animal from the infected ones and do not move, sell or give away any. Burn or bury the dead animals and any soiled litter, then disinfect the house. Vaccinate the flock with the La Sota or B1 strain in the drinking water or as an eye-drop, and repeat on the schedule given by a veterinary auxiliary. I cannot give you an exact date when breeding can resume; the veterinary auxiliary can advise you on local practices.

per_item.reference: You have Striga, also called witchweed, on your sorghum. Pull the Striga by hand before it flowers and burn what you uproot so the seed does not spread. Add organic manure and a little urea to the soil and earth up to weaken Striga and strengthen your crop. Rotate or intercrop your sorghum with a grain legume such as cowpea, groundnut or soybean to run down the seed bank. These actions are especially needed in Kara and Savanes during the growing season. history.content: My sorghum is not growing well and I see some weeds near the plants.
Do you see a purple or pink flowered weed clinging around the base of the stunted sorghum plants?
Yes, there are small purple flowers at the base of the plants.

draws.answer: You are dealing with a sorghum background with striga, a parasite that requires three special crops to control. Grow a striga tolerant sorghum variety together with or in your main sorghum crop. Grow the new sorghum in the same plot where you previously planted your normal variety. Do not grow the striga tolerant variety alone because it needs regular pollination. After harvest, cut the sorghum stems at ground level and leave the nitrogen-fixing root nodules in the soil. Then grow a cereal crop in rotation with the striga tolerant sorghum variety. If you need a variety that matches your region's season, see ICAT.

history.content: My field shows cassava leaves that are yellow and twisted, but I also notice some brown rot in the roots. Which disease am I dealing with?

draws.answer: Cassava mosaic disease shows yellow or pale mottling and leaf deformation, while cassava brown streak disease shows angular water-soaked spots on the leaves and the stems become gum-prone, and there is no leaf deformation. First, uproot and destroy any plants that are strongly mottled and stunted. Next, when you plant again, cut only from healthy-looking plants and avoid any mottled or deformed stems. Then plant a tolerant variety and rotate the plot to a cereal field. For clean tolerant cuttings you should contact ITRA. I cannot give you any other specific product details.

history.content: What steps should I take to manage Striga hermonthica in my sorghum crop?

draws.answer: Striga hermonthica is the parasitic plant that grows in the sorghum and needs to be managed before the sorghum flowers. Plant your sorghum on ridges after a heavy rain, putting 3 to 5 grains per pocket at a depth of 3 cm with 2 to 3 seeds per pocket at 3 to 5 cm. When the seedlings are 2 to 3 months old, the first weeding should be done to keep the field clear of weeds. Apply NPK fertilizer at 150 to 200 kg per hectare after weeding, then add urea at 50 to 100 kg per hectare. When the sorghum reaches panicle initiation, integrate a legume like cowpea or soybean. For any earthing-up or disease questions, see ICAT.

Striga, also called sorghum striga, is the parasitic plant that climbs and consumes the nitrogen of a sorghum plant. First, sow your sorghum on ridges after a heavy rain, placing three to five seeds per pocket at three to five centimetres depth and using six to eight kilograms of treated seed per hectare. Four to five days after sowing, treat each seed with 20-25 ml of the recommended NPK fertilizer. Then, at panicle initiation about seven to ten days after sowing, apply urea at 150 to 200 kilograms per hectare. End by consulting ICAT for the current approved product and exact rate.

history.content: My sorghum has Striga, it must be nutrient deficiency, so I just add fertilizer

draws.answer: It is not Striga, it is nitrogen loss that appears when maize is planted after sorghum and the root system of sorghum does not compete with the nitrogen-fixing roots of maize. Striga appears in the sorghum and is handled by growing a sorghum legume such as cowpea or groundnut in the same plot, pulling the striga plants out, or using a striga-tolerant sorghum variety, and it cannot be fixed by adding fertilizer. To tell them apart, look at the crop: Striga gives a dense, purple-flavored knot on the ferrari and the plant is stunted, while nitrogen loss shows window-pane holes in the leaves and the plants are short even when fertilized. For the correct solution, see ICAT.

It is not nutrient deficiency, it is Striga, a parasitic plant that climbs the stem of the sorghum to extract its nutrients. Nutrient deficiency shows a uniform pale yellowing of the older lower leaves while the top leaves stay green, and the problem spreads slowly. Striga appears suddenly in the crop and is not a disease you can cure. Because it is Striga, you need to pull it out immediately, removing any plants that have the parasite from the field. Then sow your next cycle on rich, well-drained soil and use the close spacing advised for sorghum to limit future infections. For a soil analysis and the correct fertilizer dose, see ICAT.

history.content: Would mixing two different insecticides give a stronger spray?

draws.answer: No. When insects are on a plant, the insecticides work differently and their strength does not add; what matters is which pest is there. Mixing two different products means you will know two different pests are in the plant. The label on the approved product tells you which one it is for and how to use it, and the label cannot be read by someone else. If you have not already, ask ICAT for the label of the approved product before you mix, and follow its instructions exactly.

The label tells you the approved product and its rate, and it tells you not to eat the leaves. If the insecticide changes, it changes the insect you are attacking, and that is a problem you have to handle by removing the insects and wearing gloves and boots. history.content: My sorghum is very stunted and I notice a pink weed clinging to its base, how can I fix this?

One kilogram of this mix treats about 1,500 to 2,000 plants, so use enough for your field. Apply the pinch to every young funnel and repeat the application every 8 to 10 days until the sorghum flowering. After the sorghum harvest, destroy or deep-bury the old stalks and rotate or intercrop with a legume like cowpea or soybean. If a large block is attacked at once, see ICAT for approved control.

history.content: I have sorghum that stays short and yellow, and a purple weed clings to its base, what is the cause?

draws.answer: Your sorghum is suffering from nitrogen loss because the purple-flowered Striga plant is growing around the base of the stems. Begin by opening a shallow drainage channel so water can run off the field instead of standing. After the soil drains, side-dress urea in a pocket 5-10 cm from each stem, using about 100 kg for your 0.25 ha plot, and keep the fertilizer off the plant to avoid burning. Keep the second weeding and earthing-up on schedule. If you later see streaks on veins or dead-hearts, go to ICAT for help.

Then, for the next season, plant a striga-tolerant sorghum variety, and cut the stems at ground level to keep the nodules in the soil. Keep the field weed-free to reduce other weed competition. draws.answer: A yellowing of the lower leaves from the bottom up and a shortened plant are signs of nitrogen shortage, not a disease. First, read the leaves: uniform pale yellow on the old lower leaves indicates the plant is hungry for nitrogen. Second, do not buy a broad-spectrum NPK compound and a systemic fungicide on a merchant's advice because mineral fertilizer alone often gives no extra yield on depleted soils. Third, bring organic matter back by adding manure, compost, or leaving residues in the field instead of burning them. Fourth, plant a legume such as cowpea, groundnut or soybean in the rotation and cut the stems at ground level so the nitrogen-fixing nodules stay in the soil. Finally, ask ICAT for a soil analysis and the correct dose for your plot.

history.content: My herd has sudden diarrhoea and many goats are dying quickly, almost all of them. What is happening?

draws.answer: This is a tick-borne disease, either gall sickness or redwater, transmitted by Amblyomma variegatum or Rhipicephalus (Boophilus) microplus ticks. Call the veterinary service the same day so they can identify whether it is gall sickness (caused by Anaplasma marginale) or redwater (caused by Babesia bigemina or Babesia bovis) and give the correct drug and dose. Tell the vet the urine colour you observed - yellow-brown without red points to gall sickness, while red to almost black points to redwater. Keep the sick animals in the shade with clean water and do not make them walk. Hand-pick all visible ticks on every animal in the herd. Never use the same needle on two animals. The veterinary service will provide the appropriate treatment.

Mix the leucaena with grasses and cereal crop residues to provide enough roughage for the rumen. Change the feed composition gradually over several days. Ensure the animals always have clean water and a mineral or salt source. If appetite does not recover or you see drooling, a swollen throat, or bloat, see the veterinary service.

history.content: What steps should I take against Striga hermonthica on my sorghum?

draws.answer: Striga is the plant that grows between the sorghum and the roots, and you should pull it out immediately. First, sow sorghum on ridges after a heavy rain, putting three to five seeds per pocket at three to five centimetres depth and using six to eight kilograms of treated seed per hectare. Do not sow on a first shower; wait until the rains are steady. After ten to fifteen days carry out the first weeding to reduce competition. Then apply NPK fertilizer at 150 to 200 kilograms per hectare, followed by urea at 50 to 100 kilograms per hectare, and earth up to protect the stem. If you later see Striga, go to ICAT for control measures.

Pull a few affected plants with their roots, keep them in a bag with some leaves, and do not spray anything until someone has examined them.
